For a long time "world age" was, to me, just the name of an error I got when I used `eval`
inside a function and then tried to call what I had defined. The manual calls it an advanced
topic most people never need, so I never looked further. This Discourse post changed that.
It starts from a simpler question, why dynamic languages are usually slow, and only names
world age once you already understand the problem it solves.

The point is that a compiler can only optimize what it can assume. Julia lets you redefine
almost anything, so it promises one thing in return: a running call keeps seeing the world
as it was when it started, and new definitions show up on the next call. That single rule
lets Julia compile and cache code ahead of each call, and it explains why
`invokelatest` exists. If you want the formal version, the post points to
[Belyakova et al. (OOPSLA 2020)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3428275).

[World Age for beginners: one way to compile a dynamic language](https://discourse.julialang.org/t/world-age-for-beginners-one-way-to-compile-a-dynamic-language/134402),
Julia Discourse.
